The Moon,
up close.

Earth's only natural satellite — 384,400 km away, close enough to raise our tides and light our nights, and the only other world humans have ever stood on. Here's what's up there, and how to watch it change.

One Moon, eight faces

The Moon doesn't change — the sunlight hitting it does. As it orbits Earth over 29.5 days, we see a different slice of its lit half. Drag through the cycle, or tap a phase to explore it.

The Moon in pictures

From far away it's a bright disc over mountains and city rooftops. Up close it's craters, rays and shadowed highlands. Filter the views, and tap any photo to see it big.

384,400 km
Average distance from Earth — about 30 Earths laid side by side. It drifts 3.8 cm farther away every year.
3,474 km
Diameter — a little over a quarter of Earth's. You could fit about 49 Moons inside our planet.
27.3 days
One orbit of Earth — the same time it takes to spin once, which is why we only ever see one face.
1/6 gravity
Surface gravity compared to Earth's. A 180 lb person would weigh just 30 lb up there.
−173° to 127°C
Surface temperature swing between lunar night and noon — with no atmosphere to soften it.
4.5 billion yrs
Age of the Moon, born when a Mars-sized world slammed into the young Earth and the debris gathered into orbit.

A surface that remembers everything

With no wind, no rain and no plate tectonics, almost nothing erases the Moon's history. Craters punched billions of years ago look as fresh as the day they formed — the lunar surface is a museum of the early solar system.

  • The maria
    The dark patches you see at full moon are vast plains of ancient lava — "seas" to early astronomers, though they never held a drop of water.
  • The craters
    Impact scars from asteroids and comets. Tycho, near the bottom at full moon, threw bright rays of debris over 1,500 km across the surface.
  • The terminator
    The moving line between lunar day and night. It's the best place to look through binoculars — shadows are longest and detail is sharpest there.

We've been there

On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11's lunar module Eagle touched down in the Sea of Tranquility. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent about two hours walking the surface while Michael Collins kept watch in orbit above.

Six crews landed in all. Twelve people have walked on the Moon — and their footprints are still there, undisturbed, because there's no weather to wash them away.

1969
Apollo 11 — first landing. "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."
1971
Apollo 15 — first Lunar Roving Vehicle; astronauts drive 27.8 km across the surface.
1972
Apollo 17 — the last crewed landing, and the only scientist (geologist Harrison Schmitt) to walk the Moon.

Watching the Moon well

No telescope required — though binoculars change everything.

  • 1Skip the full moon for detail. It looks flat because the Sun shines straight onto it. A crescent or quarter moon shows far more texture.
  • 2Follow the terminator. Night after night it sweeps across new craters — the Moon visibly changes every evening.
  • 3Use any binoculars. Even 7×50s reveal the maria, bright ray craters, and mountains along the shadow line.
  • 4Look for earthshine. On a young crescent, the dark part glows faintly — that's sunlight reflected off Earth, lighting the Moon.
